task.name: Forward-port unconditionally reverts pyproject.toml to main, silently dropping non-version changes
task.story_text:
## Observed behavior

The forward-port workflow reverts `pyproject.toml` and `CHANGELOG.md` to main's
copy on every port, unconditionally, whether or not the merge conflicted. Any
change to those files made on a release branch for a reason other than a version
bump or changelog roll is silently discarded in transit, and the port still
reports success.

`.github/workflows/forward-port.yml`:

```bash
# Even when the merge is clean, never let release-line version bumps
# or changelog rolls land on main.
git checkout ORIG_HEAD -- pyproject.toml CHANGELOG.md
```

`ORIG_HEAD` is main. The intent — keeping release-line `rc` versions and
changelog rolls off main — is correct and necessary. The mechanism discards the
entire file rather than the fields that must not propagate.

Observed on PR #2001 (forward-port of `release/v0.13` into `main`). #2012
narrowed the supported interpreter set, changing three things on the release
branch:

```
.github/workflows/ci.yml   python-version: ["3.11","3.12","3.13"] -> ["3.12"]
pyproject.toml             requires-python = ">=3.11"             -> ">=3.12"
pyproject.toml             [tool.ruff] target-version = "py311"   -> "py312"
```

The port carried the `ci.yml` change and discarded both `pyproject.toml`
changes. The resulting tree declares a single-version CI matrix alongside a
floor and lint target for the version that was removed.

The inconsistency was caught only because #2012 also shipped
`tests/test_apply_branch_protection.py::test_requires_python_floor_matches_ci_matrix`,
which the port did carry:

```
FAILED tests/test_apply_branch_protection.py::test_requires_python_floor_matches_ci_matrix
AssertionError: assert '>=3.11' == '>=3.12'
```

Without that test the port would have merged, and main would hold a narrowed CI
matrix with an unnarrowed floor and lint target, with no signal that anything was
lost.

## Diagnosis

**Observed symptom:** a forward-port produced a tree containing part of a change,
and the omission was detectable only by a test that happened to assert the
relationship between a file that was ported and a file that was not.

**Evidence.** The unconditional revert is the block quoted above. It runs after
the merge on every invocation, outside the `if [ "$merge_rc" -ne 0 ]` branch that
handles conflicts, so a clean merge is affected identically to a conflicted one.
The conflict branch above it does the same thing for the same two files via
`git checkout --ours`.

Confirmed by diffing the two branches directly. Three differences exist in
`pyproject.toml` between `origin/main` and `origin/release/v0.13`:

```
version           "0.12.0.dev0"  vs "0.13.0rc9"    <- the case the guard exists for
requires-python   ">=3.11"       vs ">=3.12"       <- dropped
[tool.ruff] target-version  "py311" vs "py312"     <- dropped
```

**Ruled out — a stale forward-port branch.** Regenerating the branch reproduces
the result, because the revert is part of the port itself rather than an artifact
of when the branch was last updated.

**Ruled out — a merge conflict resolved in the wrong direction.** The revert is
unconditional; no conflict is required for the loss to occur, and the workflow's
own comment states this is deliberate for the clean-merge case.

**Ruled out — long-running silent erosion.** The diff above shows the only
non-version differences are the two introduced by #2012. Nothing earlier was
lost, because until now no release-branch change had touched these files for a
non-version reason. The defect has been latent, not active.

**Confirmed cause:** the guard is scoped to files rather than to the content
that must not propagate. `pyproject.toml` holds the project version *and*
packaging metadata, tool configuration, dependencies, and test settings.
Protecting the version by reverting the file protects everything else in it from
being ported too.

**Fix-success criterion:** a forward-port carries every release-branch change to
`pyproject.toml` except the `[project] version` field, and every change to
`CHANGELOG.md` except release-roll entries; main's version and changelog remain
untouched. Given `release/v0.13` at the time of PR #2001 as input, the port
produces a main tree with `requires-python = ">=3.12"`, `target-version =
"py312"`, and main's own `version` unchanged.

## Expected behavior

A guard that exists to stop one specific thing from propagating has to be scoped
to that thing. Protecting a field by discarding the file that contains it makes
every unrelated change in that file conditional on nobody noticing, and the
broader the file's purpose the more it silently swallows — `pyproject.toml`
carries the interpreter floor, tool configuration, dependencies, and packaging
metadata alongside the version the guard is actually defending.

The stronger requirement is that dropping content must never be silent. This
workflow already distinguishes a real failure from a no-op: unresolvable
conflicts abort the port and file an issue, and an already-ported tree exits
cleanly. Discarding a change sits between those two and is reported as neither,
so a port that loses work is indistinguishable from one that carried everything.
Where an automated step decides not to propagate something, that decision is
information the operator needs, and it should be surfaced at least as loudly as
the conflicts the same workflow already refuses to guess at.

This matters more than an ordinary reporting gap because of what the workflow
guarantees. Main is documented as a strict superset of every release line, and
other work depends on that being true. A step that can quietly make it false
converts a stated invariant into an assumption that happens to hold, and there is
no way to tell which one is in force at any given moment.

handoff.summary: Replaced forward-port.yml's unconditional `git checkout ORIG_HEAD -- pyproject.toml CHANGELOG.md` (and the equivalent `--ours` on the conflict path) with a content-scoped guard, scripts/forward_port_guard.py. Its `protect` mode takes the merged tree's file and restores only main's `[project] version` and main's `[Unreleased]` changelog section, dropping the versioned sections a release roll created; every other release-branch change to those files ports through. Its `resolve` mode three-way merges a conflicted version file after normalising the version/roll scope on all three sides to main's copy, so the rc bump no longer conflicts (including by line-adjacency with requires-python) and only genuine conflicts remain. Both modes self-verify the rewrite against the merge result — a TOML round-trip comparison for pyproject, a section-by-section comparison for the changelog — and raise GuardError with a `::error::` annotation and a non-zero exit for anything they would discard outside that scope or cannot classify, which routes through the workflow's existing merge --abort -> issue + Slack failure path. The exclusion report is echoed to the job summary and referenced in the PR body. Verified end-to-end against two throwaway git repos reproducing the PR #2001 clean-merge case and a conflicted-version-file case.

story_deviations: The guard lives at scripts/forward_port_guard.py rather than under src/. Convention 7 names src/tests/docs, but this is repo release tooling invoked by a GitHub workflow, not part of the shipped theforge package; scripts/derive_changelog.py is the existing precedent for a unit-tested Python helper there. Flagging in case the reviewer wants it moved.

Plan step 2 asked to 'preserve main's release-roll-only changelog content while allowing unrelated release-branch changelog edits to remain'. Implemented as: main's [Unreleased] wins outright, sections present in main keep their merged content, version-keyed sections absent from main are dropped as rolls. A release-line edit made *inside* a rolled version section is therefore dropped with that section — it is roll content by construction and has no landing place on main. Anything not classifiable under that rule fails the port.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules
Keep modules single-purpose; extract instead of growing monolith files
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
